analysis: Switching classes of order <= 8 reproduce OEIS A002854 (1, 1, 2, 3, 7, 16, 54, 243). Under the symmetric difference no two-graph of order <= 16 has two factorisations into prime two-graphs (composite classes 1, 2, 3, 3, 7, 20, 54, 14, 246 at orders 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 16, each with exactly one factorisation); prime two-graph counts 1, 2, 2, 7, 14, 54, 240, 2035, 33113, ... (n = 2, 3, ...), not in the OEIS. K2 xor X = K2 xor Y holds exactly for switching-equivalent X, Y on all 12,713 pairs of graphs with <= 6 vertices.
assumptions: switching classes of order n <= 8 obtained from all graphs with <= 7 vertices (order 8: a 7-vertex graph plus an isolated vertex represents every class)
switching equivalence decided exactly: same Seidel spectrum, then isomorphism of descendants
class counts validated against OEIS A002854
falsification: Two different multisets of prime two-graphs with switching-equivalent XOR products.

hypothesis: H-C14-4 (bold): every two-graph of order <= 16 has exactly one factorisation into prime two-graphs under XOR. H-C14-8: K2 xor X and K2 xor Y are isomorphic graphs iff X and Y are switching equivalent (the 'if' part is proved in Theorem 7; 'only if' is tested here for orders <= 7).
methodology: Classify switching classes by order, find composite classes (orders 4, 6, 8), enumerate all multisets of prime classes with product order n in {4,6,8,9,10,12,14,15,16}, classify the XOR products up to switching, record collisions; count primes per order.
question: The symmetric difference (XOR) product respects Seidel switching (Theorem 6). On switching classes (two-graphs), is factorisation into primes unique?

summary: K2 xor X = K2 xor Y  <=>  X ~ Y: 0 violations in 12713 pairs (orders <= 6)
